CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS
                   (ENG 524)

                                             Lecture-01

                       What is Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)

Topic-01: Introduction to Discourse Analysis

   The term Discourse Analysis was first introduced by Zelling Harris (1952) to examine the
language beyond the level of the sentence, relation between linguistic and non-linguistic
behaviour. It looks at patterns of the language across texts as well as the social and cultural
contexts in the texts occur. It ranges from textually oriented views of discourse to socially
oriented views of discourse. Knowledge about language, beyond the word, clause, phrase and
sentence is needed for successful communication. The relationship between language and
context is quite significant. A pragmatic view of language is at the core of discourse analysis.

Different Views/Aspects of DA

       Discourse is the social construction of reality. Discourse and socially situated identities
are strongly related to each other. The ways we make visible and recognizable who we are and
what we are doing always involve more than just language (Gee, 2005, cited in Paltridge, 2008).
Discourse and Performance: ‘a Discourse is a ‘dance’ (Gee, 2005, p. 19). While we say
something, we also do it. Discourse and intertextuality are also relevant to each other.

Assumptions of Discourse Analysis

Four main assumptions:

a. Language is ambiguous - What things mean is never absolutely clear. All communication
involves interpreting what other people mean.

b. Language is always ‘in the world’ - what language means is always a matter of where and
when it is used and what it is used to do.

c. The way we use language is inseparable from who we are and the different social groups to
which we belong. We use language to display different kinds of social identities.

d. Language is never used all by itself. It is always combined with other things such as our tone
of voice, facial expressions and gestures when we speak, and the fonts, layout and graphics we
use in written texts.

Topic-02: Discourse and Text

        Meaning is the most important thing that makes a text; it has to make sense (Halliday). A
text, in his view, is everything that is meaningful in a particular situation. And the basis for
meaning is choice (Halliday 1978: 137). Different patterns of texture are associated with
different types of texts. Devices are structured in a conventional way with a summary of the
main points in the beginning and with the details coming later. The study of the social functions
of different kinds of texts is called genre analysis. Mitchell (1957) was one the first researchers
to examine the discourse structure of texts. He looked at the ways in which people order what
they say in buying and selling interactions. He looked at the overall structure of these kinds of
texts, introducing the notion of stages into discourse analysis; that is the steps that language users
go through. The notion of genre in discourse analysis goes beyond examining the conventional
structures and features of different kinds of texts to asking what these structures and features can
tell us about the people who use the texts and what they are using them to do. A genre is a
recognizable communicative event characterized by a set of communicative purposes. Most often
it is highly structured and conventionalized with constraints on allowable contributions in terms
of their intent, positioning, form and functional value. Three important aspects of genres:

a. Genres are communicative events

b. Conventions and Constraints

c. Creativity

        Different patterns of texture are associated with different types of texts. Newspaper
articles, for example, tend to favor particular kinds of cohesive devices and are structured in a
conventional way with a summary of the main points in the beginning and with the details
coming later (e.g. see SectionC2).

Topic-03: The Emergence of CDA

        CDS developed historically out of Critical Linguistics (CL), an approach to language
study developed at the University of East Anglia. CL emphasizes on the role of ideology and
power relations in the practice of language use and the persuasive power of syntactic forms, such
as the passive and nominalized forms (Kress 1989). Critical Discourse Studies (CDS) is an inter
disciplinary approach to language in use - how discourse figures in social processes, social
structures and social change. CDS is practiced in a wide range of fields, apart from language
studies, such as anthropology, business studies, geography, health studies, media studies,
psychology and tourism studies. CDS is not a method of discourse studies, but a group of
varying approaches each with distinctive, but also overlapping methods (Wodak and Meyer,
2016). CDA is a linguistic approach that emerged in the early 1990s and is based on the view
that discourse - including written and spoken texts -is socially determined. (CDA) is a type of
discourse analytical research that primarily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and
inequality are enacted, reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political context
(Van Dijk). Investigates how social practices, events and texts are interrelated and arise out of
and are ideologically shaped by relations of power (Fairclough, 1995).

CDA as a Method of Research

        Views the systematic analysis and interpretation of texts as potentially revelatory of ways
in which discourses consolidate power and colonize human subjects through often covert
position calls (Locke, 2004).

The Aim of CDA

        To help reveal hidden and ‘often out of sight’ values, positions and perspectives
underlying texts (Paltridge, 2008). To unmask the strategies of discriminatory inclusion and
exclusion in language in use (Wodak, 1992). The use of discourse is in relation to social and
cultural issues such as race, gender, politics, identity, ideology, etc.

Assumptions of CDA

CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS
         (ENG 524)

                                             Lecture-01

                       What is Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)

Topic-01: Introduction to Discourse Analysis

   The term Discourse Analysis was first introduced by Zelling Harris (1952) to examine the
language beyond the level of the sentence, relation between linguistic and non-linguistic
behaviour. It looks at patterns of the language across texts as well as the social and cultural
contexts in the texts occur. It ranges from textually oriented views of discourse to socially
oriented views of discourse. Knowledge about language, beyond the word, clause, phrase and
sentence is needed for successful communication. The relationship between language and
context is quite significant. A pragmatic view of language is at the core of discourse analysis.

Different Views/Aspects of DA

       Discourse is the social construction of reality. Discourse and socially situated identities
are strongly related to each other. The ways we make visible and recognizable who we are and
what we are doing always involve more than just language (Gee, 2005, cited in Paltridge, 2008).
Discourse and Performance: ‘a Discourse is a ‘dance’ (Gee, 2005, p. 19). While we say
something, we also do it. Discourse and intertextuality are also relevant to each other.

Assumptions of Discourse Analysis

Four main assumptions:

a. Language is ambiguous - What things mean is never absolutely clear. All communication
involves interpreting what other people mean.

b. Language is always ‘in the world’ - what language means is always a matter of where and
when it is used and what it is used to do.

c. The way we use language is inseparable from who we are and the different social groups to
which we belong. We use language to display different kinds of social identities.

d. Language is never used all by itself. It is always combined with other things such as our tone
of voice, facial expressions and gestures when we speak, and the fonts, layout and graphics we
use in written texts.

Topic-02: Discourse and Text

        Meaning is the most important thing that makes a text; it has to make sense (Halliday). A
text, in his view, is everything that is meaningful in a particular situation. And the basis for
meaning is choice (Halliday 1978: 137). Different patterns of texture are associated with
different types of texts. Devices are structured in a conventional way with a summary of the
main points in the beginning and with the details coming later. The study of the social functions
of different kinds of texts is called genre analysis. Mitchell (1957) was one the first researchers
to examine the discourse structure of texts. He looked at the ways in which people order what
they say in buying and selling interactions. He looked at the overall structure of these kinds of
texts, introducing the notion of stages into discourse analysis; that is the steps that language users
go through. The notion of genre in discourse analysis goes beyond examining the conventional
structures and features of different kinds of texts to asking what these structures and features can
tell us about the people who use the texts and what they are using them to do. A genre is a
recognizable communicative event characterized by a set of communicative purposes. Most often
it is highly structured and conventionalized with constraints on allowable contributions in terms
of their intent, positioning, form and functional value. Three important aspects of genres:

a. Genres are communicative events

b. Conventions and Constraints

c. Creativity

        Different patterns of texture are associated with different types of texts. Newspaper
articles, for example, tend to favor particular kinds of cohesive devices and are structured in a
conventional way with a summary of the main points in the beginning and with the details
coming later (e.g. see SectionC2).

Topic-03: The Emergence of CDA

        CDS developed historically out of Critical Linguistics (CL), an approach to language
study developed at the University of East Anglia. CL emphasizes on the role of ideology and
power relations in the practice of language use and the persuasive power of syntactic forms, such
as the passive and nominalized forms (Kress 1989). Critical Discourse Studies (CDS) is an inter
disciplinary approach to language in use - how discourse figures in social processes, social
structures and social change. CDS is practiced in a wide range of fields, apart from language
studies, such as anthropology, business studies, geography, health studies, media studies,
psychology and tourism studies. CDS is not a method of discourse studies, but a group of
varying approaches each with distinctive, but also overlapping methods (Wodak and Meyer,
2016). CDA is a linguistic approach that emerged in the early 1990s and is based on the view
that discourse - including written and spoken texts -is socially determined. (CDA) is a type of
discourse analytical research that primarily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and
inequality are enacted, reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political context
(Van Dijk). Investigates how social practices, events and texts are interrelated and arise out of
and are ideologically shaped by relations of power (Fairclough, 1995).

CDA as a Method of Research

        Views the systematic analysis and interpretation of texts as potentially revelatory of ways
in which discourses consolidate power and colonize human subjects through often covert
position calls (Locke, 2004).

The Aim of CDA

        To help reveal hidden and ‘often out of sight’ values, positions and perspectives
underlying texts (Paltridge, 2008). To unmask the strategies of discriminatory inclusion and
exclusion in language in use (Wodak, 1992). The use of discourse is in relation to social and
cultural issues such as race, gender, politics, identity, ideology, etc.

Assumptions of CDA

        Language use is always social. Discourse both reflects and constructs the social world.

                       What is Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)

Topic-01: Introduction to Discourse Analysis

    The term Discourse Analysis was first introduced by Zelling Harris (1952) to examine: the
language beyond the level of the sentence, relation between linguistic and non-linguistic
behaviour. It looks at patterns of language across texts as well as the social and cultural contexts
the texts occur. Ranges from textually-oriented views of discourse to socially-oriented views of
discourse. Knowledge about language, beyond the word, clause, phrase and sentence, needed for
successful communication. The relationship between language and context. Pragmatic view of
language at the core of discourse analysis. The discourse structure of texts. Cultural ways of
speaking and writing e.g. cultural ways of buying and selling.

Different Views/Aspects of DA

        Discourse as the social construction of reality. Discourse and socially situated identities.
The ways we make visible and recognizable who we are and what we are doing always involve
more than just language (Gee, 2005, cited in Paltridge, 2008). Discourse and Performance ‘a
Discourse is a ‘dance’ (Gee, 2005, p. 19). While we say something, we also do it. Discourse and
intertextuality.

Assumptions of Discourse Analysis

Four main assumptions:

a. Language is ambiguous - What things mean is never absolutely clear. All communication
involves interpreting what other people mean.

b. Language is always ‘in the world’ - what language means is always a matter of where and when
it is used and what it is used to do.

c. The way we use language is inseparable from who we are and the different social groups to
which we belong. We use language to display different kinds of social identities.

                                                                      Maha Malik’s Compilation

d. Language is never used all by itself. It is always combined with other things such as our tone of
voice, facial expressions and gestures when we speak, and the fonts, layout and graphics we use
in written texts.

Topic-02: Discourse and Text

        Meaning is the most important thing that makes a text; it has to make sense (Halliday). A
text, in his view, is everything that is meaningful in a particular situation. And the basis for
meaning is choice (Halliday 1978: 137). And the basis for meaning is choice. Different patterns of
texture are associated with different types of texts. Devices are structured in a conventional way
with a summary of the main points in the beginning and with the details coming later. The study
of the social functions of different kinds of texts is called genre analysis. Mitchell (1957) was one
the first researchers to examine the discourse structure of texts. He looked at the ways in which
people order what they say in buying and selling interactions. He looked at the overall structure of
these kinds of texts, introducing the notion of stages into discourse analysis; that is the steps that
language users go through. The notion of genre in discourse analysis goes beyond examining the
conventional structures and features of different kinds of texts to asking what these structures and
features can tell us about the people who use the texts and what they are using them to do. A genre
is a recognizable communicative event characterized by a set of communicative purposes. Most
often it is highly structured and conventionalized with constraints on allowable contributions in
terms of their intent, positioning, form and functional value. Three important aspects of genres:

a. Genres are communicative events

b. Conventions and Constraints

c. Creativity

        Different patterns of texture are associated with different types of texts. Newspaper articles,
for example, tend to favor particular kinds of cohesive devices and are structured in a conventional
way with a summary of the main points in the beginning and with the details coming later (e.g. see
SectionC2).

Topic-03: The Emergence of CDA

                                                                        Maha Malik’s Compilation

        CDS developed historically out of Critical Linguistics (CL), an approach to language study
developed at the University of East Anglia. CL emphasizes on the role of ideology and power
relations in the practice of language use and the persuasive power of syntactic forms, such as the
passive and nominalized forms (Kress 1989). Critical Discourse Studies (CDS) is an inter
disciplinary approach to language in use - how discourse figures in social processes, social
structures and social change. CDS is practiced in a wide range of fields, apart from language
studies, such as anthropology, business studies, geography, health studies, media studies,
psychology and tourism studies. CDS is not a method of discourse studies, but a group of varying
approaches each with distinctive, but also overlapping methods (Wodak and Meyer, 2016). CDA is
a linguistic approach that emerged in the early 1990s and is based on the view that discourse -
including written and spoken texts -is socially determined. (CDA) is a type of discourse analytical
research that primarily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and inequality are enacted,
reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political context (Van Dijk). Investigates
how social practices, events and texts are interrelated and arise out of and are ideologically shaped
by relations of power (Fairclough, 1995).

CDA as a Method of Research

        Views the systematic analysis and interpretation of texts as potentially revelatory of ways
in which discourses consolidate power and colonize human subjects through often covert position
calls (Locke, 2004).

The Aim of CDA

        To help reveal hidden and ‘often out of sight’ values, positions and perspectives underlying

18 Critical Discourse Analysis
            TEUN A. VAN DIJK

0 Introduction: What Is Critical Discourse Analysis?

Critical discourse analysis (CDA) is a type of discourse analytical research that prim-
arily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and inequality are enacted,
reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political context. With
such dissident research, critical discourse analysts take explicit position, and thus
want to understand, expose, and ultimately resist social inequality.
   Some of the tenets of CDA can already be found in the critical theory of the
Frankfurt School before the Second World War (Agger 1992b; Rasmussen 1996). Its
current focus on language and discourse was initiated with the "critical linguistics"
that emerged (mostly in the UK and Australia) at the end of the 1970s (Fowler et al.
1979; see also Mey 1985). CDA has also counterparts in "critical" developments in
sociolinguistics, psychology, and the social sciences, some already dating back to the
early 1970s (Birnbaum 1971; Calhoun 1995; Fay 1987; Fox and Prilleltensky 1997;
Hymes 1972; Ibanez and Iniguez 1997; Singh 1996; Thomas 1993; Turkel 1996; Wodak
1996). As is the case in these neighboring disciplines, CDA may be seen as a reaction
against the dominant formal (often "asocial" or "uncritical") paradigms of the 1960s
and 1970s.
   CDA is not so much a direction, school, or specialization next to the many other
"approaches" in discourse studies. Rather, it aims to offer a different "mode" or
"perspective" of theorizing, analysis, and application throughout the whole field. We
may find a more or less critical perspective in such diverse areas as pragmatics,
conversation analysis, narrative analysis, rhetoric, stylistics, sociolinguistics, ethno-
graphy, or media analysis, among others.
   Crucial for critical discourse analysts is the explicit awareness of their role in soci-
ety. Continuing a tradition that rejects the possibility of a "value-free" science, they
argue that science, and especially scholarly discourse, are inherently part of and
influenced by social structure, and produced in social interaction. Instead of denying
or ignoring such a relation between scholarship and society, they plead that such
relations be studied and accounted for in their own right, and that scholarly practices

        Visit Cluesbook.com For More Handouts And Past Papers

                                                          Critical Discourse Analysis 353

be based on such insights. Theory formation, description, and explanation, also in
discourse analysis, are sociopolitically "situated," whether we like it or not. Reflec-
tion on the role of scholars in society and the polity thus becomes an inherent part
of the discourse analytical enterprise. This may mean, among other things, that dis-
course analysts conduct research in solidarity and cooperation with dominated groups.
   Critical research on discourse needs to satisfy a number of requirements in order to
effectively realize its aims:

•   As is often the case for more marginal research traditions, CDA research has to be
    "better" than other research in order to be accepted.
•   It focuses primarily on , social problems and political issues, rather than on current
    paradigms and fashions.
•   Empirically adequate critical analysis of social problems is usually multidisciplinary.
•   Rather than merely describe discourse structures, it tries to explain them in terms of
    properties of social interaction and especially social structure.
•   More specifically, CDA focuses on the ways discourse structures enact, confirm,
    legitimate, reproduce, or challenge relations of power and dominance in society.

Fairclough and Wodak (1997: 271-80) summarize the main tenets of CDA as follows:

      1.   CDA addresses social problems
      2.   Power relations are discursive
      3.   Discourse constitutes society and culture
      4.   Discourse does ideological work
      5.   Discourse is historical
      6.   The link between text and society is mediated
      7.   Discourse analysis is interpretative and explanatory
      8.   Discourse is a form of social action.

Whereas some of these tenets have also been discussed above, others need a more
systematic theoretical analysis, of which we shall present some fragments here as a
more or less general basis for the main principles of CDA (for details about these
aims of critical discourse and language studies, see, e.g., Caldas-Coulthard and
Coulthard 1996; Fairclough 1992a, 1995a; Fairclough and Wodak 1997; Fowler et al.
1979; van Dijk 1993b).

1 Conceptual and Theoretical Frameworks

Since CDA is not a specific direction of research, it does not have a unitary theoretical
framework. Within the aims mentioned above, there are many types of CDA, and
these may be theoretically and analytically quite diverse. Critical analysis of conversa-
tion is very different from an analysis of news reports in the press or of lessons and
teaching at school. Yet, given the common perspective and the general aims of CDA,
we may also find overall conceptual and theoretical frameworks that are closely
related. As suggested, most kinds of CDA will ask questions about the way specific

discourse structures are deployed in the reproduction of social dominance, whether
they are part of a conversation or a news report or other genres and contexts. Thus,
the typical vocabulary of many scholars in CDA will feature such notions as "power,"
"dominance," "hegemony," "ideology," "class," "gender," "race," "discrimination,"
"interests," "reproduction," "institutions," "social structure," and "social order," be-
sides the more familiar discourse analytical notions.'

theoretical framework that critically relates discourse, cognition, and society.

Q. Define Context

Context refers to the circumstances surrounding a discourse, including the linguistic, situational,
social, and cultural background that influences meaning and interpretation.

Q. Definition of ideology by Althusser

Althusser defined ideology as “representing the imaginary relationship of individuals to their real
conditions of existence” which “has a material existence”.

Q. Define Conventional Implicature and Particularized Implicature

      Conventional Implicature: These do not require specific context and are derived from
       the conventional meaning of words. Examples include ‘but’ (contrast), ‘even’
       (unexpectedness), and ‘yet’ (future change).
      Particularized Implicature: These depend on the context of the conversation. The
       meaning is inferred based on situational factors and relevance.

Q. Objectives of English-Urdu Newspapers

      To explore the significance of headlines in discourse and society.
      To investigate how headlines represent the same event differently.
      To analyze how headlines influence ideological construction.
      To identify linguistic similarities and differences among various newspapers.

Q. Three Important Areas of Media CDA Under Research

      Structural conventions of media texts and language
      Representation and normalization of ideologies in media
      Sociological implications of media discourses, including capitalism, neoliberalism, and
       racism.

Q. How Ethnographic Discourse Analysis Contributes to CDA

Ethnographic discourse analysis provides a contextualized understanding of discourse by
analyzing how language is used in specific social and cultural contexts. It helps in revealing
power dynamics and ideological structures in discourse.

Q. The Discursive Study of Imran Khan’s Speech

A critical discourse analysis of Imran Khan’s 2013 election speech showed that:

Q. Foucault’s Theory of Power (in 4-5 lines)

Foucault’s theory of power suggests that power is not only centralized but also widely dispersed
across social institutions and practices. It operates through discourse and knowledge, shaping
individuals' behavior. Power is both restrictive and productive, influencing norms and self-
regulation. Resistance and counter-resistance are inherent in power relations.

Q. Cook’s View on Advertising and CDA

Cook views advertising as a persuasive discourse that shapes consumer behavior and ideologies.
CDA examines how advertisements use linguistic and visual strategies to create implicit
meanings and influence public perceptions.

Q. Three Characteristics of Corpus Analysis

      It involves analyzing large text corpora.
      It uses computational tools to examine linguistic patterns.
      It helps in identifying discourse trends over time.

Q. Four Analytical Types of Media Studies in CDA

      Structural analysis of media language
      Representation of social identities
      Ideological functions of media discourse
      Sociological implications of media messages

Q. Key Topics in Television and Discourse Studies

      Representation of gender, race, and class
      Ideological construction in news and entertainment
      Media framing and audience interpretation

Q. Positioning and Subjectivity in Media Studies and CDA

Positioning refers to how individuals are placed within discourse, influencing their identity and
perspectives. Subjectivity is the way media constructs individual identities through discourse,
shaping public perceptions and ideological stances

Q. Political discourse analysis
Political discourse analysis (PDA) involves examining the language used
in political contexts to understand how power, ideology, and political
agendas are constructed and conveyed. This type of analysis often focuses
on speeches, debates, policies, and other forms of communication used by
politicians and political institutions.
Q. Social media CDA
Social media CDA involves analyzing the content and interactions on
social media platforms to understand how discourse is shaped and how it
influences social and political opinions. It includes studying hashtags,
posts, comments, and the network of interactions among users to identify
patterns and implications of online communication.
Q. What is terrorism
Terrorism refers to the use of violence and intimidation, especially against
civilians, in the pursuit of political aims. It is characterized by its
deliberate targeting of non-combatants and its intent to create fear and
coerce governments or societies to achieve specific ideological goals.
Q. Class talk by different linguists
Class talk refers to the way language is used in classroom settings, often
analyzed by different linguists to understand how teachers and students
interact, how knowledge is constructed, and how power dynamics play
out in educational environments.

When the project is media CDA, the three strands that are often similar
include:
     Analysis of representation: How different groups, events, and issues
     are portrayed in the media.
     Analysis of media production: How media content is created,
     including the role of journalists, editors, and media organizations.
     Analysis of audience reception: How media messages are
     interpreted and understood by different audiences.
Q. 5 discourse historical strategies by Wodak
The five discourse historical strategies by Wodak include:
     Nomination: How actors, objects, and events are named and referred
     to.
     Predication: Attributing qualities, characteristics, or features to
     social actors, objects, and events.
     Argumentation: The construction and justification of arguments.
     Perspectivization: Positioning the speaker's or writer's point of view.
     Intensification and mitigation: Modifying the intensity or tone of
     statements.

Discursive strategies are the methods used in communication to achieve

Q. How Labor Party different from Conservative Party?
The Labor Party and Conservative Party differ in their political ideologies
and policies. Generally, the Labor Party is associated with social
democracy, advocating for social justice, welfare state, and public
ownership, while the Conservative Party tends to support free-market
policies, limited government intervention, and individual responsibility.

Q. Write note on covert and overt racism
Covert racism refers to subtle, often hidden, discriminatory practices and
attitudes, while overt racism is explicit and openly displayed. Covert
racism can be harder to detect and challenge, whereas overt racism is more
visible and direct.

Jessop's five approaches to examining neoliberalism include:

Perpetrator mitigation involves strategies and discourse used to downplay
or justify the actions of those who commit offenses or harmful acts. It
seeks to lessen the perceived severity of the perpetrator's actions.

What are the principles of the historiographical approach in CDA? OR Summarize the
historiographical approach in CDA? OR What does CDA need to do from a
historiographical approach?

According to the historiographical approach, CDA should:

   1) Contextualize the past – Study the past in its social context.
   2) Study production – Examine how historical discourse is created.
   3) Study reception – Examine how people understand historical discourse.
   4) Explore meanings – Analyze different meanings and interpretations of the past.
   5) Check legitimacy and distribution – Study how historical discourse gains acceptance,
      value, and spreads in society.

Definition of neoliberalism?Also True/False from this

Neoliberalism is a term that deals specifically with economic ideas about free markets.
Neoliberalism is characterized by free market trade, deregulation of financial markets,
privatization, individualization, and the shift away from state welfare provision. The neoliberal
era began in the 1970s and continues to the present. It is a specific form of free market
Capitalism that has largely come to dominate global economics. It was originally referred to as
"globalization" and began with "Free Trade deals" in the 80s and 90s. The "anti-globalization"
protests of the 90s were attempts to resist neoliberalism.

According to Flowerdew (2012) discuss historiographical approach?

According to Flowerdew (2012), the historiographical approach to Critical Discourse Analysis
(CDA) studies how history is written and explained through language. It looks for hidden
assumptions and ideas in historical accounts and shows that history is not simply a collection of
facts but is constructed through language.

Flowerdew explains that people connect their past, present, and future to understand meaning.
Historical discourses may highlight some events while ignoring others. These discourses help
people build their identity and connect with groups such as family, political groups, or a nation.
They appear in everyday conversations as well as in history textbooks. This approach also
examines how history can be used to maintain power, hide inequality, silence victims, or remove
responsibility for human rights violations. At the same time, it encourages alternative
interpretations of the past to promote critical awareness and a fairer understanding of history.

ENG524_Glossary

 1. Coherence: Coherence refers to the quality of being logical and consistent,
    e.g., 'This essay, on the whole, lacks coherence'.
 2. Context Models: Context models are special kinds of experience models.
    They represent communicative episodes in which we participate, often as part
    of other everyday episodes (conversation at breakfast, meeting at work, etc.).
 3. Conversation Analysis: Conversation analysis (CA) is an approach to the
    study of social interaction, embracing both verbal and non-verbal conduct, in
    situations of everyday life.
 4. Critical Linguistics: Critical Linguistics (CL) is “an approach to language
    study which uses linguistic techniques to investigate the ideologies (value
    systems and sets of beliefs) which underlie texts”
 5. Dialectical Relational Approach: According to Dialectical Relational
    Approach CDA is based upon a view of semiosis as an irreducible element of
    all material social processes (Williams 1977). Semiosis is viewed as an
    element of the social process which is dialectically related to others.
 6. Dialectics: The art or practice of arriving at the truth by the exchange of
    logical arguments.
 7. Discourse: Discourse is a unit of language usually longer than a sentence but
    the deduced meaning is beyond the level of sentence.
 8. Interpersonal Meanings: The interpersonal meanings are concerned with the
    interaction between speaker(s) and addressee(s).
 9. Lexicon: A lexicon is the knowledge that a native speaker has about a
    language.
 10.      Mental Model: A mental model is an explanation of someone's thought
    process about how something works in the real world.

 11.     SFL: Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) is an approach to
   linguistics that considers language as a social semiotic system.
 12.     Situation Models: Situation models represent the situation a discourse
   is about, refers to and hence may also be called semantic models.
 13.     Systematic Functional Linguistics: Systemic functional linguistics
   (SFL) is an approach to linguistics that considers language as a social semiotic
   system.
 14.     The Discourse-Historical Approach: The Discourse-Historical
   Approach considers discourse analysis not just to be a method of language
   analysis, but a multidimensional project incorporating theory, methods,
   methodology and empirically based research practices that yield concrete

CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS
         (ENG 524)

                                             Lecture-01

                       What is Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)

Topic-01: Introduction to Discourse Analysis

    The term Discourse Analysis was first introduced by Zelling Harris (1952) to examine: the
language beyond the level of the sentence, relation between linguistic and non-linguistic
behaviour. It looks at patterns of language across texts as well as the social and cultural contexts
the texts occur. Ranges from textually-oriented views of discourse to socially-oriented views of
discourse. Knowledge about language, beyond the word, clause, phrase and sentence, needed for
successful communication. The relationship between language and context. Pragmatic view of
language at the core of discourse analysis. The discourse structure of texts. Cultural ways of
speaking and writing e.g. cultural ways of buying and selling.

Different Views/Aspects of DA

        Discourse as the social construction of reality. Discourse and socially situated identities.
The ways we make visible and recognizable who we are and what we are doing always involve
more than just language (Gee, 2005, cited in Paltridge, 2008). Discourse and Performance ‘a
Discourse is a ‘dance’ (Gee, 2005, p. 19). While we say something, we also do it. Discourse and
intertextuality.

Assumptions of Discourse Analysis

Four main assumptions:

a. Language is ambiguous - What things mean is never absolutely clear. All communication
involves interpreting what other people mean.

b. Language is always ‘in the world’ - what language means is always a matter of where and
when it is used and what it is used to do.

c. The way we use language is inseparable from who we are and the different social groups to
which we belong. We use language to display different kinds of social identities.

d. Language is never used all by itself. It is always combined with other things such as our tone
of voice, facial expressions and gestures when we speak, and the fonts, layout and graphics we
use in written texts.

Topic-02: Discourse and Text

        Meaning is the most important thing that makes a text; it has to make sense (Halliday). A
text, in his view, is everything that is meaningful in a particular situation. And the basis for
meaning is choice (Halliday 1978: 137). And the basis for meaning is choice. Different patterns
of texture are associated with different types of texts. Devices are structured in a conventional
way with a summary of the main points in the beginning and with the details coming later. The
study of the social functions of different kinds of texts is called genre analysis. Mitchell (1957)
was one the first researchers to examine the discourse structure of texts. He looked at the ways
in which people order what they say in buying and selling interactions. He looked at the overall
structure of these kinds of texts, introducing the notion of stages into discourse analysis; that is
the steps that language users go through. The notion of genre in discourse analysis goes beyond
examining the conventional structures and features of different kinds of texts to asking what
these structures and features can tell us about the people who use the texts and what they are
using them to do. A genre is a recognizable communicative event characterized by a set of
communicative purposes. Most often it is highly structured and conventionalized with constraints
on allowable contributions in terms of their intent, positioning, form and functional value. Three
important aspects of genres:

a. Genres are communicative events

b. Conventions and Constraints

c. Creativity

        Different patterns of texture are associated with different types of texts. Newspaper
articles, for example, tend to favor particular kinds of cohesive devices and are structured in a
conventional way with a summary of the main points in the beginning and with the details
coming later (e.g. see SectionC2).

Topic-03: The Emergence of CDA

        CDS developed historically out of Critical Linguistics (CL), an approach to language
study developed at the University of East Anglia. CL emphasizes on the role of ideology and
power relations in the practice of language use and the persuasive power of syntactic forms, such
as the passive and nominalized forms (Kress 1989). Critical Discourse Studies (CDS) is an inter
disciplinary approach to language in use - how discourse figures in social processes, social
structures and social change. CDS is practiced in a wide range of fields, apart from language
studies, such as anthropology, business studies, geography, health studies, media studies,
psychology and tourism studies. CDS is not a method of discourse studies, but a group of
varying approaches each with distinctive, but also overlapping methods (Wodak and Meyer,
2016). CDA is a linguistic approach that emerged in the early 1990s and is based on the view
that discourse - including written and spoken texts -is socially determined. (CDA) is a type of
discourse analytical research that primarily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and
inequality are enacted, reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political context
(Van Dijk). Investigates how social practices, events and texts are interrelated and arise out of
and are ideologically shaped by relations of power (Fairclough, 1995).

CDA as a Method of Research

        Views the systematic analysis and interpretation of texts as potentially revelatory of ways
in which discourses consolidate power and colonize human subjects through often covert
position calls (Locke, 2004).

The Aim of CDA

        To help reveal hidden and ‘often out of sight’ values, positions and perspectives
underlying texts (Paltridge, 2008). To unmask the strategies of discriminatory inclusion and
exclusion in language in use (Wodak, 1992). The use of discourse in relation to social and
cultural issues such as race, gender, politics, identity, ideology, etc.

18 Critical Discourse Analysis
            TEUN A. VAN DIJK

0 Introduction: What Is Critical Discourse Analysis?

Critical discourse analysis (CDA) is a type of discourse analytical research that prim-
arily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and inequality are enacted,
reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political context. With
such dissident research, critical discourse analysts take explicit position, and thus
want to understand, expose, and ultimately resist social inequality.
   Some of the tenets of CDA can already be found in the critical theory of the
Frankfurt School before the Second World War (Agger 1992b; Rasmussen 1996). Its
current focus on language and discourse was initiated with the "critical linguistics"
that emerged (mostly in the UK and Australia) at the end of the 1970s (Fowler et al.
1979; see also Mey 1985). CDA has also counterparts in "critical" developments in
sociolinguistics, psychology, and the social sciences, some already dating back to the
early 1970s (Birnbaum 1971; Calhoun 1995; Fay 1987; Fox and Prilleltensky 1997;
Hymes 1972; Ibanez and Iniguez 1997; Singh 1996; Thomas 1993; Turkel 1996; Wodak
1996). As is the case in these neighboring disciplines, CDA may be seen as a reaction
against the dominant formal (often "asocial" or "uncritical") paradigms of the 1960s
and 1970s.
   CDA is not so much a direction, school, or specialization next to the many other
"approaches" in discourse studies. Rather, it aims to offer a different "mode" or
"perspective" of theorizing, analysis, and application throughout the whole field. We
may find a more or less critical perspective in such diverse areas as pragmatics,
conversation analysis, narrative analysis, rhetoric, stylistics, sociolinguistics, ethno-
graphy, or media analysis, among others.
   Crucial for critical discourse analysts is the explicit awareness of their role in soci-
ety. Continuing a tradition that rejects the possibility of a "value-free" science, they
argue that science, and especially scholarly discourse, are inherently part of and
influenced by social structure, and produced in social interaction. Instead of denying
or ignoring such a relation between scholarship and society, they plead that such
relations be studied and accounted for in their own right, and that scholarly practices

        Visit Cluesbook.com For More Handouts And Past Papers

                                                          Critical Discourse Analysis 353

be based on such insights. Theory formation, description, and explanation, also in
discourse analysis, are sociopolitically "situated," whether we like it or not. Reflec-
tion on the role of scholars in society and the polity thus becomes an inherent part
of the discourse analytical enterprise. This may mean, among other things, that dis-
course analysts conduct research in solidarity and cooperation with dominated groups.
   Critical research on discourse needs to satisfy a number of requirements in order to
effectively realize its aims:

•   As is often the case for more marginal research traditions, CDA research has to be
    "better" than other research in order to be accepted.
•   It focuses primarily on , social problems and political issues, rather than on current
    paradigms and fashions.
•   Empirically adequate critical analysis of social problems is usually multidisciplinary.
•   Rather than merely describe discourse structures, it tries to explain them in terms of
    properties of social interaction and especially social structure.
•   More specifically, CDA focuses on the ways discourse structures enact, confirm,
    legitimate, reproduce, or challenge relations of power and dominance in society.

Fairclough and Wodak (1997: 271-80) summarize the main tenets of CDA as follows:

      1.   CDA addresses social problems
      2.   Power relations are discursive
      3.   Discourse constitutes society and culture
      4.   Discourse does ideological work
      5.   Discourse is historical
      6.   The link between text and society is mediated
      7.   Discourse analysis is interpretative and explanatory
      8.   Discourse is a form of social action.

Whereas some of these tenets have also been discussed above, others need a more
systematic theoretical analysis, of which we shall present some fragments here as a
more or less general basis for the main principles of CDA (for details about these
aims of critical discourse and language studies, see, e.g., Caldas-Coulthard and
Coulthard 1996; Fairclough 1992a, 1995a; Fairclough and Wodak 1997; Fowler et al.
1979; van Dijk 1993b).

1 Conceptual and Theoretical Frameworks

Since CDA is not a specific direction of research, it does not have a unitary theoretical
framework. Within the aims mentioned above, there are many types of CDA, and
these may be theoretically and analytically quite diverse. Critical analysis of conversa-
tion is very different from an analysis of news reports in the press or of lessons and
teaching at school. Yet, given the common perspective and the general aims of CDA,
we may also find overall conceptual and theoretical frameworks that are closely
related. As suggested, most kinds of CDA will ask questions about the way specific

they are part of a conversation or a news report or other genres and contexts. Thus,

sides the more familiar discourse analytical notions.'

ENG524
1. Discourse Analysis (DA)

Study of language use beyond sentences, examining patterns and social contexts.

2. Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)

Focuses on how power, ideology, and social inequality are reproduced through language.

3. Zelling Harris

Introduced the term discourse analysis in 1952 to analyze language beyond sentences.

4. Pragmatics

Study of meaning in context and how language is used in social interactions.

5. Social Construction of Reality

How language shapes perceptions of reality and constructs identities.

6. Text and Context

Relationship between linguistic elements (text) and the situational background (context).

7. Genre Analysis

Examines structured patterns of language use within specific communicative events.

8. Cultural Rhetoric

How cultural norms influence language use in discourse.

9. Intertextuality

The relationship between texts where one text references or draws from another.

10. Ideology

Belief systems embedded within language that reflect power dynamics.

11. Power Relations

How authority and dominance are enacted and maintained in discourse.

12. Social Cognition

Shared mental frameworks that mediate language, society, and text.

13. Ruth Wodak

Key scholar in CDA who developed the Discourse-Historical Approach.

14. Norman Fairclough

A pioneer of CDA, focusing on the interplay between discourse, power, and ideology.

15. Teun A. van Dijk

CDA scholar emphasizing socio-cognitive aspects of discourse.

16. Socio-Cultural Approach

Framework linking discourse with social and cultural practices.

17. Discourse-Historical Approach (DHA)

Analyzes discourse in its historical, cultural, and social dimensions.

18. Socio-Cognitive Approach

Focuses on cognitive processes shared among social groups that influence discourse.

19. Nomination Strategy

Discursive practice that labels people, objects, or events in specific ways.

20. Predication Strategy

Assigning attributes to social actors or entities within discourse.

21. Argumentation Strategy

Discursive methods to validate claims and persuade others.

22. Mitigation

Reducing the impact or force of a statement in discourse.

23. Intensification

Enhancing the impact or emotional strength of a statement.

24. Genre

A socially recognized category of text or speech used for specific communicative purposes.

25. Critical Narrative Analysis (CNA)

Combines narrative and critical analysis to uncover power structures.

26. War-Normalizing Narratives

Discursive strategies that present war as a normal or acceptable state.

27. Recontextualization

Adapting discourse elements from one context to another.

28. Euphemization

Softening harsh realities using less direct language.

29. Naturalization

Presenting social phenomena as natural and inevitable.

30. Perspectivization

Positioning the speaker's or writer's viewpoint in discourse.

31. Intertextual Relationships

Connections and influences between different texts and discourses.

32. Macro-Level Analysis

Examining large-scale social structures and power dynamics in discourse.

33. Micro-Level Analysis

Focuses on smaller, detailed aspects of language use, like turn-taking in conversations.

34. Fields of Action

Contexts in which discourse operates, such as politics, media, or education.

35. Semiotic Practice

The use of signs, symbols, and language to create meaning.

36. Multimodal Discourse Analysis

Analyzing discourse across multiple modes, including visual and verbal.

37. Socio-Diagnostic Critique

Identifies ethical and social implications of discourse.

38. Prospective Critique

Application-oriented critique to improve communication practices.

39. Linguistic Description

Analyzing formal properties of text like grammar and vocabulary.

40. Discourse Practice

The production, distribution, and consumption of texts.

41. Sociocultural Practice

Connections between discourse and wider social, cultural, and political structures.

42. Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL)

Analyzes the relationship between language structure and its social functions.

43. Contextualization Cues

Signals within discourse that guide interpretation, such as tone or gestures.

44. Face and Politeness Theory

Managing self-image and respect in social interactions through discourse.

45. Identity Construction

How language creates and reflects individual and group identities.

46. Critical Theory

Framework examining societal structures and their influence on power and oppression.

47. Triangulation

Using multiple data sources or methods to validate research findings.

48. Topoi

Argumentative strategies in discourse to support claims.

49. Interdiscursivity

Blending elements from multiple discourses within a single text.

50. Textual Analysis

Detailed examination of linguistic and structural features of texts.

Q. Second Mode of Communication

The second mode of communication refers to written communication, while the first mode is
spoken communication. Written communication includes texts such as books, articles, emails,
reports, and social media posts. It is usually planned, structured, and permanent, unlike spoken
communication which is spontaneous and temporary.

Q. Pragma-Dialectics (Short Note)

Pragma-dialectics is an approach to argumentation analysis developed by van Eemeren and
Grootendorst. It studies how people use language to resolve differences of opinion through
reasonable discussion. The focus is on identifying fallacies, argument structures, and whether
arguments follow the rules of critical discussion.

Q. Discursive Strategy (Applied)

A discursive strategy refers to how language is used deliberately to achieve a social or
ideological goal. For example, calling migrants “illegal” instead of “undocumented” is a
discursive strategy that shapes public perception negatively. Thus, discursive strategies connect
language choices with power, ideology, and intention.

Q. Textual Knowledge vs Primarily Knowledge-Related Critique

Textual (or discourse-immanent) critique focuses on contradictions, gaps, presuppositions, and
inconsistencies                 within               the              text                itself.
Primarily knowledge-related critique examines whether the text misrepresents facts, history,
or social reality. In exams, this contrast shows how CDA evaluates both internal text structure
and external knowledge claims.

Q. Interpretation Stage (Standalone Explanation)

The interpretation stage in Fairclough’s 3D model explains how readers or listeners process and
understand a text. It focuses on the relationship between the text and its production and
consumption, including cognition, intertextuality, and context. Here, discourse is treated as a
discursive practice, not just language.

Q. Contextual Factors in CDA

Contextual factors in CDA include:

      Social and institutional setting
      Power relations
      Ideology
      Historical background

       Participants’ roles and identities

These factors influence how discourse is produced, interpreted, and understood. CDA treats
context as dynamic and socially constructed.

Q. Halliday & Webster: Textual Elements (Long Answer)

Halliday and Webster argue that textual meaning organizes language into a coherent and
meaningful whole. Textual elements include theme–rheme structure, cohesion, information
flow, and text organization. These elements help speakers and writers connect ideas logically
and guide readers in interpreting meaning within context.

Q. Bartlett’s Research

Bartlett’s research focused on memory and reconstruction, showing that people do not recall
texts exactly as they are but reshape them according to cultural knowledge and beliefs. In
discourse studies, his work highlights how meaning is influenced by social and cultural schemas,
not just language.

Q. Five Types to Select Text from a Corpus

Five common ways to select texts from a corpus are:

   1.   Genre-based selection
   2.   Topic-based selection
   3.   Time-based (diachronic) selection
   4.   Register-based selection
   5.   Purpose-based selection

These help ensure that corpus data is relevant and representative.

Q. Macgilchrist’s Strategies

Macgilchrist identified counter-discursive strategies such as:

       Parody
       Logical inversion
       Complexification
       Partial reframing
       Radical reframing

These strategies challenge dominant discourses by re-presenting social reality differently.

Q. Cameron’s Views

                                  Mid-Term (Solved)

Deborah Cameron views language as a social practice shaped by power, ideology, and identity.
She argues that discourse is not neutral and that linguistic choices reflect gender, politics, and
social inequality. Her work connects discourse with everyday social life.

Q. Pragmatics

Pragmatics studies meaning in context. It explains how speakers convey meanings beyond literal
words through implicature, presupposition, speech acts, politeness, and inference. Pragmatics
is important in CDA because it reveals hidden meanings and ideological assumptions.

Q. Naturalization + Justification

Naturalization presents social actions or events as normal, inevitable, or natural, hiding human
agency.
Justification portrays actions as reasonable, necessary, or morally right.
Together, they legitimize power and ideology in discourse.

Q. Three Proofs in Rhetoric

According to Aristotle, the three proofs in rhetoric are:

      Ethos – credibility of the speaker
      Pathos – emotional appeal to the audience
      Logos – logical reasoning and evidence

Write "Three maxim of Grice" (3)
Here are the Three Maxims of Grice:
1. Utterance Maxim: Make your contribution as informative as is required for the
current context.
2. Quality Maxim: Be truthful in your communication.
3. Quantity Maxim: Be brief in your communication, avoiding unnecessary
elaboration or detail
"What are discursive strategies?" (3)
According to Reisigl and Wodak (2009), discourse strategy is an intentional plan
of discursive practices and tactics employed in discourses to achieve a particular
social, political, psychological or linguistic goal.
"What are the five tenets of Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA)?" (5)

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                               1

Fairclough introduced the concepts that are now viewed as vital in CDA such as
"discourse, power, ideology, social practice and common sense." He argues that
language should be analyzed as a social practice through the lens of discourse in
both speaking and writing.
"What is Positive Discourse Analysis, and how does it differ from other forms
of discourse analysis?" (5)
Positive Discourse Analysis (PDA) is a subfield of discourse analysis that focuses
on the ways in which language is used to create positive social change. Unlike
other forms of discourse analysis, which often focus on power dynamics and
language use in social contexts, PDA is specifically concerned with identifying and
promoting positive language practices that can contribute to social justice and
equality. For example, PDA may involve analyzing language use in educational
settings to identify ways in which teachers can promote positive social change
through their language use.
"What are four assumptions made by Jewett?" (5)
1. People are born with a blank slate, without any inherent abilities or knowledge.
2. Learning is a process of adding new information to what you already know,
rather than replacing or modifying existing knowledge.
3. Learning is an active process, requiring effort and engagement from the learner.
4.Learning is a gradual process, with progress occurring over time and with
repeated practice.
How is identity defined and studied? (3)
Identity refers to an individual's organized constellation of traits; attitudes; self-
knowledge; cognitive structures; past, present, and future self-representations;
social roles; relationships; and group affiliations.

"What are three common figures of speech?" (3)

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                                   2

1. Metaphor: A comparison between two things that are not alike, but share a
common quality. For example, "My life is a rollercoaster ride."
2. Simile: A comparison between two things using "like" or "as." For example, "He
runs like a cheetah."
3.Personification: Attributing human qualities or characteristics to non-human
things. For example, "The sun smiled down on us."
What is the significance of stance and engagement in the context of discourse
analysis? (3)
Stance and engagement are important rhetorical resources for writers to construct
interaction with readers and ideas by marking epistemic evaluation and bringing
readers into the texts.

basic principles or tenets of CDA Some are as follows: (i) CDA addresses social

"What is the concept of transitivity in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL)
and how does it impact the analysis of language?" (5)
In Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL), the system of Transitivity is a common
means by which to analyse both isolated clauses as well as clauses in context. To
date, two Transitivity models have emerged. Systemic functional linguistics treats
grammar as a meaning-making resource and insists on the interrelation of form and
meaning.

discourse- historical analysts (Wodak, 2009: 1). These are critique, ideology and
power. The DHA adheres to the sociophilosophical orientation of critical theory.

Critical Discourse Analysis
Introduction: What Is Critical Discourse Analysis?
Critical discourse analysis (CDA) is a type of discourse analytical research that
primarily studies the way social power abuse, dominance, and inequality are
enacted, reproduced, and resisted by text and talk in the social and political
context. With such dissident research, critical discourse analysts take explicit
position, and thus want to understand, expose, and ultimately resist social
inequality. Some of the tenets of CDA can already be found in the critical theory
of the Frankfurt School before the Second World War (Agger 1992b: Rasmussen
1996). Its current focus on language and discourse was initiated with the "critical
linguistics" that emerged (mostly in the UK and Australia) at the end of the 1970s
(Fowler et al. 1979, see also Mey 1985). CDA has also counterparts in "critical"
developments in sociolinguistics, psychology, and the social sciences, some
already dating back to the early 1970s (Himbaum 1971; Calhoun 1995; Fay 1987:
Fox and Frilleltensky 1997: Hymes 1972: Ibanez and Iniguez 1997; Singh 1996;
Thomas 1993; Turkel 1996, Wodak 1996). As is the case in these neighboring
disciplines, CDA may be seen as a reaction against the dominant formal (often
"asocial" or "uncritical") paradigms of the 1960s and 1970s. CDA is not so much a

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                            1

direction, school, or specialization next to the many other "approaches" in
discourse studies. Rather, it aims to offer a different "mode" or "perspective" of
theorizing, analysis, and application throughout the whole field. We may find a
more or less critical perspective in such diverse areas as pragmatics, conversation
analysis, narrative analysis, rhetoric, stylistics, sociolinguistics, ethnography, or
media analysis, among others. Crucial for critical discourse analysts is the explicit
awareness of their role in society. Continuing a tradition that rejects the
possibility of a "value-free" science, they argue that science, and especially
scholarly discourse, are inherently part of and influenced by social structure, and
produced in social interaction. Instead of denying or ignoring such a relation
between scholarship and society, they plead that such relations be studied and
accounted for in their own right, and that scholarly practices.
Fairclough and Wodak (1997: 271-80) summarize the main tenets of CDA as
follows:
1. CDA addresses social problems
2. Power relations are discursive
3. Discourse constitutes society and culture
4. Discourse does ideological work
5. Discourse is historical
6. The link between text and society is mediated
7. Discourse analysis is interpretative and explanatory 8. Discourse is a form of
social action.
Whereas some of these tenets have also been discussed above, others need a
more systematic theoretical analysis, of which we shall present some fragments
here as a more or less general basis for the main principles of CDA (for details
about these aims of critical discourse and language studies, see, eg, Caldas-
Coulthard and Coulthard 1996; Fairclough 1992a, 1995a; Fairclough and Wodak
1997, Fowler et al. 1979, van Dijk 1993b).
Conceptual and Theoretical Frameworks

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                              2

Since CDA is not a specific direction of research, it does not have a unitary
theoretical framework. Within the aims mentioned above, there are many types
of CDA, and these may be theoretically and analytically quite diverse. Critical
analysis of conversation is very different from an analysis of news reports in the
press or of lessons and teaching at school. Yet, given the common perspective and
the general aims of CDA, we may also find overall conceptual and theoretical
frameworks that are closely related. As suggested, most kinds of CDA will ask
questions about the way specificdiscourse structures are deployed in the
reproduction of social dominance, whether they are part of a conversation or a
news report or other genres and contexts. Thus, the typical vocabulary of many
scholars in CDA will feature such notions as "power," "dominance," "hegemony."
"ideology," "class," "gender," "race," "discrimination," "interests," "reproduction."
"institutions," "social structure," and "social order," besides the more familiar
discourse analytical notions. In this section. I focus on a number of basic concepts
themselves, and thus devise a theoretical framework that critically relates
discourse, cognition, and society.
Macro vs. micro
Language use, discourse, verbal interaction, and communication belong to the
micro level of the social order. Power, dominance, and inequality between social
groups are typically terms that belong to a macro level of analysis. This means
that CDA has to theoretically bridge the well-known "gap" between micro and
macro approaches, which is of course a distinction that is a sociological construct
in its own right (Alexander et al. 1987: Knorr-Cetina and Cicourel 1981). In
everyday interaction and experience the macro- and microlevel (and intermediary
"mesolevels") form one unified whole. For instance, a racist speech in parliament
is a discourse at the microlevel of social interaction in the specific situation of a
debate, but at the same time may enact or be a constituent part of legislation or
the reproduction of racism at the macro level. There are several ways to analyze
and bridge these levels, and thus to arrive at a unified critical analysis:
1. Members-groups: Language users-engage in discourse as members of (several)
social groups, organizations, of institutions; and conversely, groups thus may act
"by" their members.

Introduction to Discourse Analysis: Discourse analysis examines how
language, both spoken and written, enacts social and cultural perspectives and
identities. It explores the intersections between language, critique, power, and
ideology. James Paul Gee's integrated approach combines a theory of
language-in-use with a method of research
 Discourse and Text
    - Text refers to any written or printed material conveying information,
       such as books, articles, or emails.
    - Discourse encompasses not only the text itself but also the broader
       context (social, cultural, historical) influencing communication
 The Emergence of CDA: Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) emerged as a
cross-disciplinary methodological and theoretical approach. It explores the
intersections between discourse, critique, power, and ideology. CDA gained
prominence in education research, examining educational policy, literacy
education, and identity
 Key Scholars of CDA
    - James Paul Gee: Introduced CDA and emphasized the role of
       language-in-use.
    - Ruth Wodak: Developed the discourse-historical approach (DHA) that
       considers historical context in discourse analysis.
    - Teun A. van Dijk: Contributed to sociocognitive approaches and
       explored dominant discourses in information systems
 Approaches of CDA
    - Sociocognitive (SCA)
    - Discourse-historical (DHA)
    - Social semiotic/multimodal (MCDA)
    - Foucauldian dispositive analysis (DPA)

      - Corpus linguistic (CorpLingA)
      - Cognitive linguistic (CogLing)
   Cultural Approach to Critical Discourse Analysis (CCDA): CCDA
  examines cultural codes, discursive strategies, and the role of culture in
  shaping discourse. It emphasizes understanding power dynamics and ideology
  within cultural contexts
  DHA: DHA considers historical context and explores how discourse reflects
  power relations and social structures
   History of Discourse Historical Approach (DHA): The DHA was initially
  developed in 1986 to examine anti-Semitic stereotypes and prejudiced
  attitudes in Austrian public discourse. Over time, it evolved to analyze
  structures of discrimination, control, and domination in European institutional
  discourse
   General Characteristics and Research Interests of DHA: The DHA views
  discourse as a system of thought, knowledge, or communication that
  constructs our experience of the world. It emphasizes the relationship between
  discourse and power, making it a valuable window into understanding societal
  dynamics. Researchers using DHA explore how language shapes reality,
  focusing on topics like migration, identity, climate change, and new media
   Discursive Strategies in DHA
DHA identifies five key discursive strategies involved in constructing and
perpetuating hegemonic discourses:
      - Nomination: Labeling and categorizing entities.
      - Predication: Making statements about entities.
      - Argumentation: Presenting reasons or justifications.
      - Perspectivization: Shaping viewpoints.
      - Intensification or mitigation: Emphasizing or downplaying aspects
   The Concept of Critique: Critique involves disciplined, systematic study of
  written or oral discourse. It goes beyond fault-finding and negative judgment;
  it can also recognize merit and involve methodical doubt. In social theory,
  critique provides insights into power dynamics and societal control
   The Concept of Discourse: Discourse extends beyond mere conversation to
  any form of communication. It constructs our understanding of the world and

is a major topic in fields like sociology, anthropology, and philosophy.
Discourse is inescapable and shapes individual perspectives
 The Concept of Context: Context refers to the broader environment in
which discourse occurs. It includes immediate co-text, intertextual
relationships, social variables, and historical dimensions. Context
significantly influences how language is used and interpreted
 Theoretical Position of CDA: CDA examines how language reflects power,
ideology, and social structures. DHA is a flexible and productive variety of
CDA, always opting for a problem-oriented perspective
Discourse and Socio-cultural Change: Discourse plays a crucial role in
shaping societal norms, values, and transformations. Analyzing changes in
discourse helps understand shifts in cultural and social contexts
 Textual Analysis in Social Research: Textual analysis examines written or
spoken texts to uncover underlying meanings, ideologies, and power
dynamics. Researchers use various methods to explore discourse in social
research
 Definition of Context: Context encompasses the situational, cultural, and
historical factors that influence communication. It provides the backdrop for
understanding discourse
 Early Models of Context: Early models of context focused on immediate
co-text and linguistic features. However, contemporary approaches consider
broader sociopolitical and historical contexts
 Recent Models of CDA: Recent models emphasize the interplay between
language, power, and social structures. They explore how discourse reflects
and perpetuates societal norms and inequalities
Genre: Genre refers to specific types of discourse with shared conventions,
purposes, and structures. Examples include academic papers, news articles,
and advertisements
 Choice and Constraints in the Use of Genre: Writers make deliberate
choices when selecting genres based on their communicative goals and
audience expectations. Constraints within genres shape how information is
presented

 Relationship between Genres: Genres are interconnected and influence
each other. For instance, news reporting may influence political speeches, and
vice versa
 Genre Analysis and Various Forms of Writing: Genre analysis examines
how different genres function in specific contexts. It helps uncover underlying
ideologies and power dynamics within written and spoken texts
 Steps in Genre Analysis: Genre analysis involves identifying genre
conventions, examining textual features, and considering the social context in
which the genre operates

          Critical Discourse Studies in Applied Contexts

Topic-01: The Applied Principles of CDS

What are some economic shifts discussed in Critical Discourse Studies (CDS)?

Examples: "post-Fordism," "information society," "knowledge economy," "liquid
modernity," "neoliberalism," and "network society."

How does Fairclough (1999) describe the communication rise in economic
exchange?

Fairclough uses the term "textual mediation" of social reality.

What is the concept of "new textualization of work" according to Iedema and
Scheeres (2003)?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                          1

Answer: It refers to workers in the modern era speaking and writing in ways not
directly associated with their work.

Name some scholars known for tracking language's role in post-industrial
commodification.

Examples: Norman Fairclough, Deborah Cameron, Monika Heller.

According to Lin (2014), what are three areas where CDS is deployed in applied
linguistics?

Answer: i) Studies of textbooks and school curricula, ii) School leadership and
student identities, iii) Public-media discourse.

What is the founding ideal of Critical Discourse Studies (CDS)?

Answer: To improve people's lives and deeply understand social change through
critiques.

According to Fairclough and Wodak (2010), what are some core principles of
CDS?

Answer: Addressing social problems and socially committed research treating
discourse analysis as a mode of social action.

Topic-02: The Limits of CDS and Applied Linguistics

What is a common criticism of CDS regarding power dynamics?

Answer: It tends to locate power in elite domains like medical, legal, media, and
corporate settings.

According to Thurlow, what domains of language expertise are often
overlooked in CDS?

Answer: Dialect coaches, voice-over artists, speech writers, campaigners,
technical writers, copy-editors, PR officers, and advertising copywriters.

What is Cameron's critique of micro-analytic approaches to institutional talk?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                              2

Answer: They don't properly account for how workplace discourse is structured
by normative systems of regulation and surveillance.

What question arises concerning workers' priorities in working with language?

Answer: What are the concerns of workers when it comes to working with
language?

Topic-03: New Directions for Critical Discourse Studies

According to Thurlow (2018), what is needed for institutionalized critique to be
effective?

Answer: It needs to invoke discourses recognized within the social practice it
critiques.

What is CDS principally committed to, in addition to social critique?

Answer: Exposing gaps in academic orthodoxy and identifying them as
ideological/hegemonic.

What area of language use does Cook (2008) suggest for further CDS
exploration?

Answer: Advertising.

What does Pennycook (1990) advocate for in critical applied linguistics?

Answer: To be more humble, listen to alternative views, and avoid preaching
views as the newest and best.

Topic-04: Conclusions

According to Theo van Leeuwen, what is essential for the effectiveness of work
in CDS?

Answer: Work needs to be recognized within the sites of intervention and valued
by more than just linguists.

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           3

What does Foucault (1977) argue about theoretical work in relation to practice?

Answer: Theoretical work is not separate; it is an activity conducted alongside
those struggling for power.

How does Deleuze (1997) characterize the usefulness of a theory?

Answer: A theory must be useful and functional; if not used, it is worthless.

Lecture-20

                              CDA and History

Topic-01: Introduction

What is the historiographical approach to critical discourse analysis (CDA)?

According to Flowerdew (2012), historiographical CDA seeks to reveal hidden
assumptions in historical accounts, emphasizing language's role in their
elaboration.

What does Flowerdew emphasize regarding the construction of meanings of the
past?

Flowerdew emphasizes that exploring the construction of meanings of the past
involves focusing on representations and receptions of discourses.

How does Flowerdew view the past in terms of construction?

Flowerdew argues that the past is not pre-existing; it has to be constructed
through semiotic work, requiring social actors' involvement in identity-building
processes.

What is the objective of a critical perspective in historiographical CDA?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                             4

The objective is to construct a past quotable in all moments, making visible
hegemonic and counter-hegemonic narratives that form part of larger power
struggles.

In what social practices do discourses about the past occur?

Discourses about the past occur in everyday practices like sharing anecdotes in a
family and more institutionalized practices such as the writing of history
textbooks.

Topic-02: Memory, history, and historiography

What is the key focus of historiography?

Historiography focuses on the construction of historical discourse, with a key
emphasis on representation as an issue in constructing discourse about the past.

How does Mariana Achugar differentiate between memory and history?

Memory is connected with lived experience (testimony), while history is more
related to the reformulation of this experience into a scientific discourse.

What is the role of memory in relation to the past?

Memory attempts to be faithful to the past, representing lived time and space,
while history aims to be truthful and represents the locus of enunciation of the
historian.
